To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nitrate and sulfate, released from nitrocelluloses and CaSO4, enhanced the natural rates of in situ anaerobic biotransformation of phenanthrene by marine bacteria in undisturbed sediment.

the rates of anaerobic in situ biodegradation of 14C- phenanthrene were enhanced by the addition of controlled-release nitrate, and to a lesser degree sulfate, in whole and interval marine sediment cores.

nitrocelluloses and CaSO4 formulations can be designed to release nitrate and sulfate, respectively, at rates that are consistent with bacterial utilization, and that the controlled-release of both electron acceptors enhances the natural anaerotic phenanthrene degradation in marine sediments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new remediation strategies for marine sediments contaminated with organic compounds.
the development of a novel remediation technology for the treatment of organic pollutants in sediments and soil by the use of controlled-release electron acceptor amendments.
the biogeochemistry and microbiology of marine sediments, specifically, the biodegradation of hydrocarbons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

nitrate and sulfate can be used to enhance anaerobically the biodegradation of hydrophobic organic contaminants (such as PAHs) in marine sediment, although the sulfate reduction may be inhibited by high nitrate concentrations.
the controlled-release of nitrate and/or sulfate enhanced the natural anaebolic biodegradation of the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, phenanthrene, in undisturbed sediments.

controlled-release of nitrate or sulfate enhanced in situ biodegradation of 14C- phenanthrene in anoxic marine harbor sediments, and nitrocelluloses were effective controlled-release formulations for the electron acceptors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the addition of nitrate to the sediments enhanced the rate of phenanthrene biotransformation.
controlled-release of nitrate and (to a lesser degree) sulfate enhances the anaerobic microbial biodegradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in marine sediments.

the use of controlled-release nitrate or sulfate may be a useful approach to enhance the in situ anaerobic biotransformation of hydrophobic organic contaminants in marine sediments, and may also provide a means to reduce the release of contaminants from sediments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the controlled release of nitrate or sulfate to enhance the anaerobic degradation of phenanthrene is a promising approach to decontaminating harbor sediments.
nitrate is more efficient in enhancing biodegradation than sulfate, and that nitrocelluloses may be a useful capping material for decontaminating marine harbor sediments.
controlled-release of nitrate and/or sulfate may enhance the anaerobic degradation of phenanthrene, a common marine contaminant, in harbor sediments.
